items.title: Non-price coordination remains a live option
items.discrepancy_analysis: The idea is reused but detached from Neurath's accounting apparatus. Benanav retains the conceptual rejection of price-based coordination but does not reconstruct the technical methods—the in-kind accounting procedures, material flow tables, and utility metrics—that Neurath embedded in his alternative. This leaves the claim floating without its original infrastructure.
items.what_benanav_misses: The sophisticated accounting techniques that made non-price coordination legible and operationalizable in Neurath's framework.

items.title: Administration becomes logistics
items.discrepancy_analysis: The institutional thickness is simplified into a logistics metaphor. Neurath's vision of administration encompassed not just material flow but social decision-making, worker participation, and the coordination of conflicting needs. Benanav's shift to logistics language—rooted in supply-chain optimization—evacuates the democratic and deliberative dimensions.
items.what_benanav_misses: The political economy of administration: how coordination decisions are made, by whom, and according to what norms of distribution and participation.

items.title: Accounting remains backgrounded
items.discrepancy_analysis: The accounting dimension is present but underdeveloped. Benanav invokes 'usable social information' as a prerequisite for coordination but does not specify the institutions, procedures, or contested methodologies of public accounting that Neurath detailed. Accounting is treated as a technical given rather than a political site.
items.what_benanav_misses: Neurath's detailed proposals for public accounting bodies, transparency requirements, and the controversies around accounting standards that bear directly on whose needs get counted and how.

items.title: International coordination is carried forward
items.discrepancy_analysis: The global horizon is retained but routed through contemporary supply-chain language. Neurath's internationalism was rooted in peace, anti-imperialism, and the coordination of production according to human need across borders. Benanav's supply-chain framing evacuates the anti-imperialist and peace-oriented politics embedded in Neurath's vision.
items.what_benanav_misses: The anti-imperialist critique and peace economics that grounded Neurath's case for international planning; contemporary supply-chain language does not carry these political commitments.

items.title: Non-price coordination remains a live option
items.implication_for_argument: It broadens the conceptual space beyond market coordination. However, without reconstruction of the accounting apparatus, the argument remains aspirational rather than institutionally grounded. Readers may accept the premise while remaining unconvinced of its feasibility.

items.title: Administration becomes logistics
items.implication_for_argument: That simplification makes the planning case easier to transpose to contemporary contexts and less institutionally demanding. However, it also strips away the participatory and democratic dimensions that Neurath insisted were central to non-capitalist coordination. The argument becomes more technically elegant but less politically substantive.

items.title: Accounting remains backgrounded
items.implication_for_argument: The result is more schematic than Neurath's original account. This creates a vulnerability: the argument can be challenged on the grounds that it underspecifies how information is gathered, validated, and used to make distributive decisions. The political contests over accounting standards—who decides what counts as a 'need'—remain invisible.

items.title: International coordination is carried forward
items.implication_for_argument: It prevents the planning case from collapsing into national developmentalism and preserves the universalist horizon. However, the loss of the anti-imperialist and peace-oriented framing may blunt the argument's force in contexts where resource conflicts and geopolitical competition are salient. The supply-chain language can appear depoliticized.
